questions.stem: A second year student of MAMC is doing a project under Dr Gobind. He has developed a protein that binds to CD3 and blocks its interaction with TCR, which is composed of γ and δ subunits. Of the following, which organ is the student studying?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C. Intestine

The TCR (T-cell receptor) binds to the MHC (major histocompatibility complex) on antigen-presenting cells, with CD4 in helper T cells and CD8 in cytotoxic T cells participating. TCR is normally composed of an α and a β subunit, however, T cells with a TCR composed of a γ and δ subunit are found associated with mucosal surfaces (gastrointestinal and urogenital tracts).

questions.stem: A 38-year-old female presents to the emergency room. She has recently been feeling weak and fatigued, unable to work out at the gym as she normally has in the past. Her trip to the emergency room is because she developed double vision today. Physical examination reveals ptosis. A CT scan of her body reveals a mass in the upper portion of the mediastinum. Of the following, what is the most likely mechanism for her conditions?

options.label: A
options.text: IgE-mediated release of inflammatory mediators from mast cells and basophils

options.label: C
options.text: Formation of immune complexes that deposit in tissues, triggering inflammation

options.label: D
options.text: Activation of T cells with recruitment of macrophages and cytokine release.

questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Antibody-dependent target cell dysfunction

 

Clinical Clues:

 

  • 38-year-old female
  • Fatigue, ptosis, diplopia (double vision)
  • Recent decline in muscle endurance
  • Mass in anterior mediastinum

 

These are classic features of Myasthenia Gravis (MG).

 

Pathophysiology of Myasthenia Gravis:

 

  • MG is caused by autoantibodies against the acetylcholine receptors (AChR) at the neuromuscular junction.
  • This is not a cytotoxic attack, nor does it involve destruction by complement.
  • Instead, antibodies block the receptor or increase its degradation, leading to functional impairment.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. IgE-mediated release of inflammatory mediators from mast cells and basophils: This describes type I hypersensitivity, like allergies and anaphylaxis - not relevant here.

 

Option C. Formation of immune complexes that deposit in tissues, triggering inflammation: Seen in diseases like SLE or post-streptococcal GN - not MG.

 

Option D. Activation of T cells with recruitment of macrophages and cytokine release: Relevant in diseases like Type 1 diabetes or contact dermatitis, but MG is primarily antibody-mediated.

 

Educational Objective: 

 

Anterior Mediastinal Mass: This is likely a thymoma, which is commonly associated with Myasthenia Gravis (present in ~15% of cases). The thymus plays a role in autoantibody production in MG.

questions.stem: A 40 year old man has chronic cough with fever for several months. The chest radiograph reveals a diffuse reticulonodular pattern. Microscopically on transbronchial biopsy there are focal areas of inflammation containing epithelioid cell granuloma, Langhans giant cells, and lymphocytes. These findings are typical for which of the following type of hypersensitivity immunologic responses:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D. Type IV

Presence of epitheloid cell granuloma, langhans giant cells and lymphocytes is characteristic of chronic granulomatous inflammation, which is associated with type 4 HR.

questions.stemHtml: Match the following with the correct names:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) A→3, B→4, C→1, D→2 

 

A. Master regulator immune system → 3. CD4 T Cell: CD4 T cells are often termed the “master regulators” of the immune system because they help activate and direct other immune cells.

 

B. Most important APC → 4. Dendritic cell: Dendritic cells are the most potent antigen-presenting cells (APCs), essential for initiating T-cell responses.

 

C. Non-nucleated cell with MHC I → 1. Platelets: Platelets are non-nucleated and have been found to express MHC I molecules.

 

D. Cell affected in SLE → 2. Red cells: In Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE), autoimmune destruction of red blood cells (among other cells) is common.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old male receives a kidney transplant from a deceased donor. Six weeks after the transplantation, he develops fever, graft tenderness, and a rise in serum creatinine levels. A kidney biopsy reveals mononuclear cell infiltrates with mild interstitial edema and endothelial cell swelling in the renal parenchyma. Immunofluorescence shows C4d deposition in peritubular capillaries. Which of the following best describes the type of transplant rejection observed in this patient?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C. Acute antibody-mediated rejection

The key characteristic that helps differentiate acute antibody-mediated rejection from other types of rejection is the immunofluorescence finding of C4d deposition in peritubular capillaries. C4d is a complement split product that indicates the activation of the classical complement pathway, which occurs in the presence of antibody-antigen complexes.

questions.stem: A 65-year-old male with acute myeloid leukemia undergoes an allogeneic stem cell transplant using bone marrow from his HLA-matched sibling. A few weeks after the transplant, he develops a skin rash, diarrhea, and mild liver dysfunction. Which of the following best describes the most likely cause of these symptoms?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B. Graft-versus-host disease (GVHD)

Graft-versus-host disease (GVHD) is a common complication following allogeneic stem cell transplantation. It occurs when donor T cells recognize the recipient's tissues as foreign and mount an immune response against them. GVHD primarily affects organs with high epithelial cell turnover, such as the skin, gastrointestinal tract, and liver.

questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C. Negative selection of T- cells in the thymus

Negative selection of T- cells in the thymus is a mechanism of central tolerance. Autoimmune diseases would develop only when there is failure of tolerance. So, the answer.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not an autoimmune disorder?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A. Ulcerative colitis

Ideally, at least three requirements should be met before a disorder is categorized as truly caused by autoimmunity:

  1. The presence of an immune reaction specific for some self antigen or self tissue;
  2. Evidence that such a reaction is not secondary to tissue damage but is of primary pathogenic significance; and
  3. The absence of another well-defined cause of the disease.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the most serious organ involvement in amyloidosis?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Renal tissue

 

Amyloidosis of the kidney is the most common and potentially the most serious form of organ involvement.

 

Other Options: 

 

Option A. Cardiac tissue: Amyloidosis of the heart may occur in any form of systemic amyloidosis. It is also the major organ involved in senile systemic amyloidosis.

 

Option C. Splenic tissue: Amyloidosis of the spleen may be inapparent grossly or may cause moderate to marked splenomegaly (up to 800 g). For completely mysterious reasons, one of two patterns of deposition is seen. In one, the deposits are largely limited to the splenic follicles, producing tapioca-like granules on gross inspection, designated sago spleen. In the other pattern, the amyloid involves the walls of the splenic sinuses and connective tissue framework in the red pulp. Fusion of the early deposits gives rise to large, map like areas of amyloidosis, creating what has been designated lardaceous spleen.

 

Option D. Hepatic tissue: The deposits may be inapparent grossly or may cause moderate to marked hepatomegaly. Amyloid appears first in the space of Disse and then progressively encroaches on adjacent hepatic parenchymal cells and sinusoids. In time, deformity, pressure atrophy, and disappearance of hepatocytes occur, causing total replacement of large areas of liver parenchyma. Vascular involvement is frequent. Even with extensive involvement, liver function is usually preserved.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Grossly, the kidneys may be of normal size and color, or, in advanced cases, they may be shrunken because of ischemia caused by vascular narrowing induced by the deposition of amyloid within arterial and arteriolar walls.

 

Histologically, the amyloid is deposited primarily in the glomeruli, but the interstitial peritubular tissue, arteries, and arterioles are also affected. The glomerular deposits first appear as subtle thickenings of the mesangial matrix, accompanied usually by uneven widening of the basement membranes of the glomerular capillaries.

 

In time, the mesangial depositions and the deposits along the basement membranes cause capillary narrowing and distortion of the glomerular vascular tuft. With progression of the glomerular amyloidosis, the capillary lumens are obliterated, and the obsolescent glomerulus is flooded by confluent masses or interlacing broad ribbons of amyloid

 

Ref: Robbins 10th edition 263-264
